headline: Asia keeps selling the AI chain as new US chip rules land on Nvidia day
tone: Risk-off overnight: Asia took Wall Street's chip sell-off a step further, and only steadier US futures stop it looking like a rout before Nvidia reports after tonight's US close.
body: Tokyo, Seoul and Taipei, home to the region's biggest AI-linked firms, took the brunt again. SoftBank Group, an OpenAI investor, lost 6.2% and test-equipment maker Advantest 4.3%; Samsung Electronics fell 2.4% while SK Hynix edged up, so investors are trimming, not dumping, memory.

The new driver is policy, not just Nvidia's leadership crisis. The US Commerce Department's rule makes data-centre operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil get a licence before shipping high-end US AI chips to clients, closing the route Chinese developers used to rent Nvidia computing power. That hit Southeast Asian and Chinese data-centre names; Saxo called it a meaningful escalation because it moves curbs from buying chips to renting them.

Nvidia's board says it is not considering bringing Jensen Huang back, so the whole weight now sits on tonight's guidance. UBS puts the options-implied move at about 7.8% and says a strong beat is already expected; the test is whether debt-funded AI spending holds into 2027 and how much of the China-linked overseas demand the new rule removes.

The dollar firmed on bets on further Fed hikes and oil slipped even after more tankers were hit in Hormuz, the same pattern as Monday: the market is trading risk appetite and the supply surplus, not Gulf supply. US retail sales this afternoon are the next check on whether the economy can carry stocks if tech stalls.

views.text: Priced in for today: more caution, with US futures holding up better than Asia. What would turn it: Nvidia guidance that shows overseas data-centre demand survives the licensing rule, or a clear CEO succession plan. A soft guide would hit the banks and miners that fund and supply the AI build-out next, as Monday afternoon showed.
Still trading the surplus, not the war. Only lost loadings at Gulf terminals or a halt to Hormuz traffic would bring the risk premium back.
